This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of this form is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parent, guardian, or next of kin is not known, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. The laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions which have been promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard. CERTIFICATE OF SCHOOL PHYSICIAN. I therefore recommend that the said child be enrolled in this school. This 7th day of Nov., 1919 School Physician. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Yakima Agency, Ft. Simcoe, Wash., Nov. 6, 1919. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt. Cushman School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: Doris and William Doyle are allotted on this reservation and their lands are held in trust. I am not prepared to say just how far they do live from a public school because my understanding is that they have been off of the reservation for some time. Furthermore, I do not believe their people could pay a tuition fee because they are poor, but at the same time I hardly believe they are the class of Indians entitled to education at the expense of the government. Very truly yours, Don M. Gary Superintendent. DMC B Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Dec. 3, 1919 The Honorable The Commissioner of Indian Affairs Washington, D. C. My dear Mr. Commissioner: Doris and William Doyle are blood Indians allotted on the Yakima Reservation. Their lands are held in trust. They are orphans, aged and respectively. Their grandmother who is unable to support them while attending public school lives six miles from the nearest public school. These children have attended Cushman two years and a half and have just returned to complete the eighth grade work. Their land, now practically valueless, will be under water by next summer, it is expected and these two children intend to return to the reservation and to develop the land and make homes for themselves on the reservation. Your approval is respectfully requested to their remaining in school until they complete the eighth grade. Very respectfully, Superintendent. MHH:MD THE CUSHMAN INDIAN SCHOOL. Tacoma, Washington. August 19th, 1919. Miss Dorris Doyle, Moxie City, Washington. Dear Miss Dorris: Recent amendments to the School Rules make it necessary for me to drop you and your brother, Willaq, from our roll, very much to my regret as both of you have been exemplary pupils in your conduct and in your school work. Only wards of the government, possessing 1/4 degree of Indian blood may be admitted, and certain conditions govern their admission. With very best wishes for your welfare and that of your brother, I am Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Yakima Agency, Pt. Simcoe, Wash. August 18, 1919. Mr. Ernest H. Hammond, Supt., Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: I have not heard from Mr. LeRoy about soliciting pupils, but it is agreeable with me for him to do so. The Doyle children are hardly eligible, strictly speaking, to enrollment at Cushman, but if it could be managed it would, no doubt, be to their interest to remain at school. I note what you say about Alice Shahaha. She was apprehended at Umatilla and sent to Chemawa before I knew anything about it. I really do not believe she is a proper pupil for any school now. I think the regulation should be waived as to her returning to Cushman because she was previously enrolled there and I hope you can see your way to concur therein. Very truly yours, Don M. Carr Superintendent. Toppenish, Wash. Sept. 3, 1919. Tacoma, Wash., Lushkman School, Mr. Hammond. Dear Sir; I would like to know about fair and the arrangements. William was very glad to receive his arrow head was thankful for the boy that found it. When shall we return to the school? We couldn't come back until after the fair anyway and we will not able to know them. Your Truly, Miss Doris Doyle. Toppenish, Wash. Gen. Del. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 5, 1919 Miss Doris Doyle Toppenish, Wash. Dear Doris: I was glad to hear from you as two letters mailed to your former address at Moxie were returned. I am sorry to inform you that I shall have to drop you from our enrolment as you are [redacted] Indian and live within reach of the public schools. If you and Willie are wards of the Government with allotments of your own, I could receive you provided you did not possess public school facilities at home. During the Fair, Mr. Carr and I were planning to have a cooking class the last three days of the Fair and I wanted, and still want you, to be one of our demonstrators. Sincerely yours, Superintendent. ERH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 3, 1919 Miss Doris Doyle Wapato, Wash. Dear Miss Doris: On August 8th, I wrote to Willie and you, addressing the letters to Moxie City, but these letters were returned. Under the new regulations, it will be impossible for me to keep you and Willie at school without special permission from the Commissioner unless you are able to pay all or part of the tuition. Please talk this over with Mr. Carr and both of us will see what can be done towards securing the consent of the Commissioner to your continuing in school. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MC Moxee City, Wash. Aug. 20, 1918. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Cushman Agency, Tacoma, Wn. Dear Mr. Hammond, Will you please let William and Doris Doyle stay with us until after the third cutting of alfalfa hay? We need their help very much on account of labor shortage. If you are willing to do this please let us know at once. and oblige, Mrs. F. Cook (Moore City, Wash.) VACATION REQUEST FOR PUPIL. We, the undersigned, respectfully request that leave of absence be granted ____________________________ __________________________ & ________________ from June 15, 1918 to September 6th, 1918 to enable them to visit their home. We hereby agree to pay all expenses, including round-trip railroad fares, sleeping-car fares, meals, lodging, stage fares, telegraph and telephone messages, and other incidental expenses connected with the visit. We further agree that said pupil shall be returned to the Cushwaas school on or before the last day of the leave of absence. We further agree to deposit with the superintendent of the school sufficient money to defray all expenses to be incurred, and should the pupils, or any one of them, fail to return to school at such time as may be agreed upon by the parents or guardian and the superintendent of the school in which the pupils are enrolled, the amount of money remaining with the superintendent, necessary to the return transportation of the pupil or pupils so neglecting to return, shall be forfeited to the Government; provided, however, that in all cases where it can be shown that there were justifiable reasons for the failure of the return of the pupil the forfeiture of the funds shall not take place. If the pupil neglecting to return is from a reservation, the superintendent of the reservation shall certify to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils. I understand that Lorrie has brother eligible for enrollment. If so, I will be glad to have him. Very respectfully, Superintendent. MIII (KM) CCushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington, November 12, 1918. The Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Washington, D.C. Sir: Attached hereto is a letter from Doris Doyle requesting the privilege of attending Cushman Trades School, for herself and brother who possess [blacked-out] degree of Indian blood. The are ambitious children and if given an opportunity will, I feel convinced, do full justice to it. They live six miles from any school and are supported by their grandmother. I recommend that they be regularly enrolled in the Cushman Trades School. Very respectfully, Superintendent. EHH - F Cushman Trades School, Tacoma, Washington, Nov. 11, 1917. Mr. Commissioner, Washington, D.C. Dear Mr. Sells: Willie and I are [blacked-out] Indian from White Swan, Yakima. When we came here Mr. Hammond said we could stay until other Indians needed our place and now we must go if you do not agree to let us stay. I like Cushman and so does Willie and we want to stay here to learn something which we can't do if we go back to White Swan which is six miles to a public school. And my grandma can not afford to send us to school any more. I am grade sixth and Willie grade seven. Please let us stay. Oblige, Doris Doyle. Copy - F - Cushman Trades School, Tacoma, Washington, Nov. 11, 1917. Mr. Commissioner, Washington, D.C. Dear Mr. Sells: Willie and I are [blacked out] Indian from White Swan, Yakima. Dear Mr. Carr: Doris and William Doyle came to school this morning for re-enrollment. I had already advised them in writing that they were ineligible for re-enrollment on the ground that they were [blacked out] bloods and citizens. They insist however, that they are wards of the Government in that they are allotted on the Yakima reservation in their own right; that they have not received their patents in fee nor can they receive them until they are of age and that they live not less than 3 1/2 miles from the nearest school. If they are allotted on the Reservation, I can receive them in spite of the ir [blacked out] blood, even if their natural guardians are full citizens. A letter from you early in September advised me that they were citizens. If there is any way in which I can legitimately give Doris and William one more year in school, I am sure it will meet with your approval. Please write me regarding the status of their allotment on the Yakima. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG RECORD OF PUPIL IN SCHOOL Record of Lewis Doyle at Cushman School.
